newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook - Cocoa eyes hurdle, coffee sideways.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook - Cocoa eyes hurdle, coffee sideways.

text.p: Cocoa futures are likely to maintain a slow ascent this week after a recent stormy ride, but the 1,087-1,108 stg chart gap basis September is a big obstacle, traders said on Monday.
The downside was limited following a low of 1,000 stg a tonne, the bottom of the current range. The market would be on guard for any crop news, and a major dampener would be sterling's strength.
Elsewhere, coffee would continue to trade sideways with origin selling keeping a firm lid on the upside. White sugar was also rangebound on a lack of significant news.
Cocoa regained some ground last week after a wild gyration the week before, which saw prices losing a sharp 170 stg within three days.
September ended Friday 15 down at 1,040, well below the week's high of 1,063 but still up from the July 3 low of 1,000.
Analysts said a technical rebound against a background of oversold conditions was taking market towards the March-April high of 1,072 or beyond. But sellers were said to be lurking at the chart gap.
Traders were keeping a close watch on crop developments in West Africa. So far the crop looked quite favourable, and that factor had probably been priced into the market.
"The other problem is how the El Nino weather system is going to affect the crop," said a senior executive at a western chocolate firm.
"At this stage it is difficult to tell if the impact would be at the same magnitude as in 1982-83, which caused severe drought in cocoa regions."
He put the Ivorian 1996/97 crop (including mid-crop) at over 1.0 million tonnes but below the record 1.2 million in 1995/96.
Global demand for cocoa was expected to remain strong, rising at 2.0-2.5 percent on an annualised basis but slower than 3-4 percent growth that some expected, he said.
But the main depressing factor was sterling's strength.
The currency jumped to above three German marks for the first time in more than 6-1/2 years on Friday. Against the Swiss franc, the pound had appreciated by 20 percent over the past two years.
"Manufacturers outside the sterling territory could suffer as the cost component in local currency terms rises," said one trader.

In coffee, dealers said the market could trade sideways with a downside bias on Asian and African selling. European roasters were comfortable with stocks in hand, and there had been an increase in the supply pipeline after the aggressive buying that followed the recent price rally.
"I see more source (origin) selling. The market will stay sideways, a little lower maybe. I don't see new fund/spec involvement and there are not signals they are going short either," one said.
The market was also awaiting U.S. June green coffee stocks data and LIFFE's certified stock number due to be released on Tuesday.
Robusta futures have been locked in a triangle chart formation with prices hovering above $1,696 support but beneath $1,850 resistance, all basis September.
Coffee lost some ground late last week after the U.S. Department of Agriculture restated a crop of 28 million bags for Brazil in 1997/98 after its attache in Sao Paulo put output at 24 million.
After a lacklustre week, LIFFE sugar looked set to remain rangebound. "I don't see the market breaking out," one said.
"Whites lack news," he said. Raws would lead the way, but would not move far before running into selling by Brazil.
The market remained bearish on fundamentals for the rest of the year. But further out it had "El Nino fever," he said. "It's like an 11th commandment. Thou shalt not sell 1998 months."
Over the past few days, expiring front month August has occupied much of the spotlight. That should end with its expiry on July 16.
